shell.title: AgroFarm
shell.tagline: Decision support for crop growth and rotation planning.
shell.disclaimer: This tool supports farmers and local experts. It never replaces local agronomic judgment.
shell.disclaimerShort: Supports your decisions. Consult a local agronomist.

tour.step1Desc: Access farm profiles, uploaded farm data, weather scenarios, crop recommendations, and climate history from the sidebar.
tour.step2Desc: Inspect your active farm or switch parcels. Registered farmers can add new parcels with custom geographic boundaries.
tour.step3Desc: Check verified hectares, current crop rotation, and the interactive geographic zone map.
tour.step4Desc: Jump directly to data uploads, weather stress simulations, agronomic rotation rankings, and NASA POWER climate data.
tour.step5Desc: Switch between dark and light themes at any time, or exit the demo session when finished.

landing.title: Plan the season before the rain does
landing.intro: See how rain, heat and El Nino could change your maize, and which rotation holds up best.
landing.demoNote: Example farm near Guatemala City. No account needed.

evidence.title: Evidence-based advice
evidence.description: Ground-level soil data, NASA POWER weather statistics, and satellite vegetation indices tailored to your farm.

uncertainty.title: Honest uncertainty ranges
uncertainty.description: Simulations clearly present confidence intervals and probabilistic projections rather than false certainties.

support.title: Supports local experts
support.description: Empowers agronomists and farmers with clear risk indicators and explicit reminders for local validation.

what.title: Try a season before you live it
what.body1: Guatemalan smallholders plan each season with rain that arrives early, late or not at all. AgroFarm takes a farm's own data, adds public weather, soil and satellite records, and estimates how a crop could grow under different conditions, including El Nino and La Nina years.
what.body2: It then compares several crop rotations side by side, such as maize followed by beans or by a fallow year. Every result is a range with its reasons, its evidence and its gaps, so a farmer and a local agronomist can discuss it and decide.

data.title: Bring the farm's data
data.description: Upload plots, soil tests and past harvests. The tool checks what was accepted and says what is missing.

scenario.title: Choose a season
scenario.description: Move rainfall, temperature and the El Nino or La Nina phase to see how the likely yield range shifts.

compare.title: Compare rotations
compare.description: Strategies are scored with the priorities you set: water, income, soil and more.

decide.title: Read the reasons and the limits
decide.description: Each recommendation shows its evidence, its risks and what we do not know. The decision stays with you.

crops.title: The crops AgroFarm compares
crops.intro: Four options for a plot, from planting maize to leaving the land to rest. Each one gives something and asks for something in return.
crops.cacaoCredit: Photo: Daderot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

maize.name: Maize
maize.description: A cereal. It sells well and needs plenty of water. It does not add nitrogen to the soil.

black_beans.name: Black beans
black_beans.description: A legume. It adds nitrogen to the soil and needs less water than maize.

cover_crop.name: Cover crop
cover_crop.description: Grown to protect the soil. Best against erosion, with little income.

fallow.name: Fallow
fallow.description: Letting the plot rest. It needs no water and brings no income, and the bare soil is exposed.

cacao.name: Cacao (not modelled yet)
cacao.description: A tree crop, very sensitive to rain and heat. We show it as the kind of crop this approach should reach later.

compare.title: How they compare at a glance
compare.note: A longer bar means more of it. Water is a cost, not a prize: more water needed is not better.
compare.source: Illustration with the starting values of the team's crop table (version 0.1.0). They are provisional and not yet checked against sources. They are not measurements of your farm.

hero.rangeTitle: Maize yield versus a normal year
hero.scene: A rendered ear of maize with its husk peeled back and golden kernels in tidy rows

principles.title: What we promise, and what we do not

finalCta.title: See it with an example farm
finalCta.body: The demo needs no account. It loads a pilot farm near Guatemala City so you can move the sliders and read a real comparison.

journey.title: From the field to one decision

field.title: The weather
field.body: AgroFarm starts wide: the rain, the heat and the El Nino or La Nina phase expected for your area.

plant.title: The plant
plant.body: Then it looks at the crop. Satellite readings of how green the plants are tell how a season is going.

cob.title: The harvest
cob.body: It estimates the yield as a range compared with a normal year, never as a single promised number.

decision.title: The decision
decision.body: Last it compares rotations and shows its reasons, risks and gaps. Then you and your agronomist decide.

journey.scene: A maize ear that turns and moves closer as you scroll, then its kernels pop out

decisions.title: Decisions this helps you make
decisions.intro: Each question below is one the demo can already help you think through. The last column says where the tool stops.

rotate.question: Maize again, or rotate to beans?
rotate.shows: Several rotations side by side, each scored with your priorities for water, income and soil.
rotate.limit: Your market prices and your own plot history are yours to weigh.

dry.question: Is a dry El Nino season too risky?
dry.shows: How the likely yield range moves when you lower rainfall or switch the El Nino or La Nina phase.
dry.limit: It cannot say when the rain will fall, only how the range shifts.

fallow.question: Should a plot rest this year?
fallow.shows: The fallow option next to the planted ones, with the reasons it ranks where it does.
fallow.limit: Local soil tests and an agronomist must confirm it.

doubt.question: How much can I trust this answer?
doubt.shows: The evidence behind each result, the data that is missing and the risks, written in plain words.
doubt.limit: It never replaces a visit from someone who knows your land.

drawer.intro: Everything below comes from a rule-based comparison that uses a provisional table of crop traits. The traits have not been reviewed by an agronomist yet. Use this as support for your decision, and check it with a local expert before you change what you plant.
drawer.noLink: No link is available for this source.
drawer.termsHint: Hover, focus or tap a term to see what it means.
drawer.glossaryNote: These plain-language definitions are drafts and still need an agronomist's review.

maize.name: Maize
maize.happens: Takes a lot of water and sells well. It uses up nitrogen, so the soil needs something that gives it back.

black_beans.name: Black beans
black_beans.happens: Puts nitrogen back into the soil and needs less water than maize. It sells reasonably well.

cover_crop.name: Cover crop
cover_crop.happens: Covers the ground, so rain washes away less soil. It brings little or no income this season.

fallow.name: Fallow
fallow.happens: The plot rests: no water is used and there is no income. The bare soil is open to rain and washing away.

detail.mapIntro: The same plot in each season. The pattern shows what is growing on it.
detail.mapLabel: Your farm seen from above in {{season}}: {{crop}}
detail.mapLoading: Loading the map of your farm...
detail.noMap: This farm has no map outline yet, so the plot cannot be drawn.

evapotranspiration.label: Evapotranspiration
evapotranspiration.definition: The water that leaves the field in two ways at once: it evaporates from the soil and the crop's leaves release it as vapor. It is measured in millimeters (mm) of water, like rain.

ndvi.label: NDVI
ndvi.definition: A vegetation index: a number from satellite images that shows how green and healthy the plants in a field look. Low values mean bare soil or stressed plants, high values mean thick, healthy plants.

soil_moisture_anomaly.label: Soil moisture anomaly
soil_moisture_anomaly.definition: How much wetter or drier the soil is than it usually is at this time of year. A negative value means drier than normal.

frost_risk.label: Frost risk
frost_risk.definition: The chance that temperatures fall low enough to damage crops. It depends on the place and on the season, so local knowledge matters.

water_balance.label: Water balance
water_balance.definition: Rain and irrigation that come in, minus the water the crops and soil use up or lose. When more leaves than comes in, plants can run short.

percentile.label: Percentile
percentile.definition: A way to show a range of outcomes: the 10th percentile is a low outcome, the 50th is the middle estimate, and the 90th is a high outcome.

enso.label: ENSO
enso.definition: El Nino-Southern Oscillation: a Pacific Ocean temperature cycle (El Nino, La Nina, or Neutral) that shifts seasonal rainfall in Central America.

reanalysis.label: Reanalysis
reanalysis.definition: A gridded weather dataset built by combining past observations with a weather model. It represents a ~50 km area, not a single farm rain gauge.

uploads.title: Upload your farm data
uploads.intro: Send a CSV or GeoJSON file with your parcels and seasons. The server checks it and stores the rows that pass.
uploads.notice: Uploaded data is checked and stored, but it is not used yet. Recommendations, scenarios and model results do not change because of it. This tool supports decisions and does not replace local agronomic judgment.

template.body: The template is a CSV file with one column for each field the server reads. A cell left empty means the value is not known. It is never read as zero.

template.columns: Dates use YYYY-MM-DD. Numbers use a decimal point. Units: area in ha, yield in kg/ha, rainfall in mm, soil nutrients in mg/kg, organic matter in %.

vegetation.title: How green the crops could look from space
vegetation.intro: Estimate regional cropland greenness using the rainfall, temperature and ENSO controls above. This is a conditional scenario, not parcel yield, crop growth or an ENSO forecast. The original validation goal was not reached.
vegetation.validation: Whole-year validation ({{years}} years): {{skill}}% improvement against climatology; the {{goal}}% goal was not reached. Interval coverage: {{coverage}}% versus nominal 80%. Annual mean correlation: {{correlation}}. Local review is required.
vegetation.caption: Seasonal peak NDVI anomaly against the cell’s own normal (%)
vegetation.cell: Reference cropland cell: {{cell}}, {{distance}} km from the farm centre; approximately 0.05 degrees. This regional cell includes mixed land cover.
vegetation.outside: Outside training range: {{inputs}}. Treat this estimate with extra caution.
vegetation.attributions: What changed the median model estimate
vegetation.explanation: These SHAP differences explain the raw median model, not causes. Rainfall changes apply uniformly across the season. ENSO phases assume RONI +1, 0 or −1 in seasonal and preseason inputs. Quantile sorting can move the raw median.
vegetation.delta: Explained raw median change: {{delta}} percentage points.

stressTest.caveatWithModel: These are per-crop results from {{model}} ({{version}}), an illustrative rule-based model — not a full rotation evaluation and not a forecast.
stressTest.tableCaption: Crop stress test matrix (median and 10th to 90th percentile yield anomaly)
stressTest.summaryEqual: All tested crops return identical estimates under the current rule-based model.
stressTest.summaryDiffers: Each scenario highlights the most resilient crop and each crop marks its worst scenario.

realityCheck.title: Climate reality check
realityCheck.subtitle: What happened here in past El Nino and La Nina years?
realityCheck.insufficient: Not enough overlapping data for 1995-2025 (NASA POWER months: {{nasaCount}}, ENSO months: {{ensoCount}}, excluded years: {{excluded}}).
realityCheck.seasonSummary: May-October wet season across {{years}} years (1995-2025). All-years average: {{mean}}. Excluded years (missing > 2 months): {{excluded}}.
realityCheck.yearDetail: In {{year}} (dominant phase: {{phase}}), May-October rainfall was {{rain}} (mean ONI: {{oni}}, missing months: {{missing}}).
realityCheck.groupDetail: In the {{count}} {{phase}} years ({{years}}), mean May-October rainfall was {{mean}} ({{diff}} vs overall average).
realityCheck.selectPrompt: Select a phase group or a year above to inspect its May-October rainfall.

presetCheck.same_direction_close: Preset "{{presetName}}" ({{presetRain}}) goes in the same direction as the observed {{count}}-year average ({{observed}}) and is fairly close, though individual years vary widely.
presetCheck.same_direction_partly: Preset "{{presetName}}" ({{presetRain}}) goes in the same direction as the observed {{count}}-year average ({{observed}}), but the magnitude differs: the data only partly supports this assumption.
presetCheck.diverges: Preset "{{presetName}}" ({{presetRain}}) differs in direction from the observed {{count}}-year average ({{observed}}): the data does not support this assumption here.
presetCheck.insufficient_data: Preset "{{presetName}}" ({{presetRain}}) cannot be reliably checked because only {{count}} years are in this group (observed: {{observed}}).

realityCheck.limitations: Limitations: NASA POWER is a ~50 km reanalysis grid cell (14.59, -90.53), not a local weather station. ENSO alone does not explain any single year's rainfall, and the sample size (n) per group is small.
